questions.stem: Under which Article of the Constitution is the office of the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) of India established?

options.option_text: Article 124
Article 148
Article 280
Article 324

questions.explanation: Article 148 establishes the office of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India. Article 124 deals with the Supreme Court; Article 280 with the Finance Commission; Article 324 with the Election Commission. The CAG is a CONSTITUTIONAL authority, described by Dr. Ambedkar as 'the most important officer under the Constitution of India'.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The CAG is appointed by which of the following?

options.option_text: The Prime Minister
The President of India by warrant under his hand and seal
A collegium of Supreme Court judges
The Parliament by a special majority

questions.explanation: Article 148(1): The CAG is appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal. The President acts on the advice of the Cabinet. There is no collegium or Parliamentary selection involved — making it an executive appointment, though the removal procedure provides judicial-level security of tenure.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: What is the term of office of the CAG?

options.option_text: 5 years or 65 years of age, whichever is earlier
6 years or 65 years of age, whichever is earlier
7 years or 67 years of age, whichever is earlier
Until retirement at 62 years

questions.explanation: Per the CAG's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971: term is 6 years or until 65 years of age, whichever is earlier. He can resign at any time by addressing the letter to the President. After retirement, he is NOT eligible for any further office under the Union or State governments — a safeguard for independence.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: How can the CAG be removed from office?

options.option_text: By the President at his pleasure
In the same manner and on the same grounds as a Supreme Court judge
By a simple majority in Parliament
By the Prime Minister with the President's approval

questions.explanation: Article 148(1) + 124(4): The CAG can be removed in the same manner as a Supreme Court judge — on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity, by an order of the President, after an address by each House of Parliament supported by a majority of the total membership AND a two-thirds majority of members present & voting. This stringent procedure ensures independence. He does NOT hold office at the President's pleasure.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The salary and conditions of service of the CAG are:

options.option_text: Determined by the President
Determined by Parliament; charged on the Consolidated Fund of India
Determined by the Finance Commission
Linked to the pay scale of a Union Minister

questions.explanation: Article 148(3): Salary and other conditions of service of the CAG shall be such as may be determined by Parliament by law. Under the CAG Act 1971, the CAG receives a salary equal to that of a Supreme Court judge. Importantly, the salary is CHARGED on the Consolidated Fund of India — meaning it is not subject to vote in Parliament (a safeguard against legislative pressure).
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The CAG submits his audit reports relating to Union accounts to:

options.option_text: The Prime Minister
The President, who causes them to be laid before each House of Parliament
The Lok Sabha Speaker directly
The Finance Minister

questions.explanation: Article 151(1): CAG's reports relating to the accounts of the Union are submitted to the President, who causes them to be laid before each House of Parliament. State reports go to the respective Governor. The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) of Parliament then examines the reports — making the CAG's work a fundamental pillar of Parliament's financial accountability over the executive.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Dr. B. R. Ambedkar described the CAG as:

options.option_text: 'The financial conscience of the nation'
'The most important officer under the Constitution of India'
'The guardian of the public purse'
'The eye of Parliament'

questions.explanation: During the Constituent Assembly debates, Dr. Ambedkar famously said the CAG 'is probably the most important officer under the Constitution of India', ranking the office alongside the Supreme Court and the Election Commission for safeguarding constitutional democracy. 'Guardian of the public purse' is a description often used for the PAC, not specifically by Ambedkar for the CAG.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Which of the following types of audit does the CAG perform?

options.option_text: Only financial (regularity) audit
Only compliance audit
Financial/Regularity audit, Compliance audit, AND Performance audit
Only performance audit

questions.explanation: CAG's audits include: (1) FINANCIAL/REGULARITY audit — whether money was spent in accordance with the budget and rules; (2) COMPLIANCE audit — whether expenditure followed legal/constitutional provisions; (3) PERFORMANCE audit — whether government programmes achieved intended objectives with economy, efficiency, and effectiveness (examples: 2G Spectrum, CWG, CoalGate audits). All three are integral parts of CAG's mandate.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: After retirement, which of the following offices is the CAG prohibited from holding?

options.option_text: Any post under the Government of India or any State
Any academic post in a private university
Any position in an international organisation like the UN
Any role as an arbitrator in civil disputes

questions.explanation: Article 148(4) / CAG Act 1971: After retirement, the CAG shall not be eligible for any further office either under the Government of India or under any State Government. This is intended to prevent the incumbent from being influenced during tenure by post-retirement job prospects. International/UN posts, private academic posts, and private arbitration are NOT prohibited (e.g., former CAG Vinod Rai became chair of the BCCI's Committee of Administrators, appointed by the SC, not the government).
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The audit of accounts of Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) is conducted by the CAG under which provision?

options.option_text: Sole auditor under Section 139 of the Companies Act 2013
Sole auditor, Supplementary auditor, or Auditor by arrangement, depending on the PSU's structure
Only an advisor to the private auditors of PSUs
No role — PSUs are audited only by chartered-accountant firms

questions.explanation: CAG's audit role for PSUs varies by structure: (a) for DEPARTMENTAL COMMERCIAL UNDERTAKINGS (e.g., Railways), CAG is the SOLE auditor; (b) for STATUTORY CORPORATIONS (e.g., LIC pre-2000, ONGC pre-1976), CAG's role depends on the enabling Act — sole, supplementary, or by arrangement; (c) for GOVERNMENT COMPANIES under Companies Act 2013 (Section 143(5)), CAG appoints the CA auditor and can conduct supplementary/test audits. So CAG's role is nuanced, not a one-size-fits-all.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Who was the first Comptroller and Auditor General of India after independence?

options.option_text: V. Narahari Rao
A. K. Roy
K. Sankar Aiyar
T. V. Ramanathan

questions.explanation: V. Narahari Rao served as the first CAG of independent India from 1948 to 1954. He was instrumental in setting up the Indian Audit and Accounts Service structure. A. K. Roy succeeded him (1954–60). K. Sankar Aiyar served later (1960–66). The current CAG (as of 2026) is Girish Chandra Murmu, who took office in August 2020 for a 6-year term.
